memories.content: Avoid em dashes in the proposal; split the sentence or use more ordinary punctuation instead.
The user tends to place several independently reviewable claims in one long sentence.
Use first-person active voice for choices and commitments owned by the proposal author so responsibility remains explicit throughout the work plan.
Describe prototype operations that have already been implemented and verified as observed states.
Describe prototype operations not yet implemented or evaluated as plans or expectations.
When a commitment is phrased passively, readers may interpret it as uncertainty, evasiveness, or reluctance to take responsibility.
Use “we” only for decisions and commitments the authors control, not for external facts or actions owned by another party.
The user should use one first-person pronoun consistently for the same authorial role and should not alternate between “I” and “we” unless the responsible party actually changes.
The user tends to hide unsettled commitments behind passive phrases such as “will be considered” or “is expected.”
Split proposal prose into short sentences when a sentence contains more than one independently reviewable claim.
Keep one main claim in each sentence so a reviewer can locate and assess it quickly.
The user tends to repeat em dashes when a sentence already contains several clauses.
Repeated em dashes can shift a reviewer’s attention from the proposal’s argument to suspicion that its prose was generated by AI.
Mark unverified schedule assumptions as such.
Mark unverified recruitment assumptions as such.
Mark unverified technical assumptions as such.
Trace back the resources required for each core prototype feature and field research procedure.
Operations reviewers judge feasibility by examining the personnel required for each procedure.
Operations reviewers judge feasibility by examining the equipment required for each procedure.
Operations reviewers judge feasibility by examining the time required for each procedure.
Document separately the commitments and confirmation status of field partners required for recruitment, installation, and operational support.
Designate a responsible party for software updates, equipment inspections, and user support during the deployment period.
The user's deployment readiness can be assessed only when dependencies on external services and field personnel are visible.
Field schedules and assigned personnel may change due to operational factors beyond the researcher’s control.

analysis.overview: Both frames favor evidence-calibrated wording and explicit responsibility. The reference additionally concentrates on sentence structure, punctuation, voice, and pronoun discipline, while the compared frame adds operational resource tracing and visibility into external field dependencies. No incompatible policies appear.

relations.reason: The reference distinguishes observed prototype states from unimplemented plans, while the compared frame requires unverified schedule, recruitment, and technical assumptions to be labeled; these jointly support evidence-calibrated wording without asserting identical scopes.
relations.summary: Prototype statements and operational assumptions should be worded according to whether they have been implemented, evaluated, or verified.

relations.reason: The reference assigns author-controlled choices and commitments to active first-person agency and excludes externally owned actions from “we,” while the compared frame requires a responsible party for deployment support duties.
relations.summary: Responsibility should be explicit for commitments and operational duties controlled by an identified party.

relations.reason: These memories form one reference-only punctuation claim comprising the observed tendency, recommended correction, and reviewer-facing consequence.
relations.summary: The reference identifies recurring em-dash-heavy proposal prose and recommends ordinary punctuation or sentence splitting to avoid distracting reviewers and suggesting AI-generated writing.

relations.reason: These memories form one reference-only sentence-structure claim comprising the observed tendency and two closely aligned editing rules.
relations.summary: The reference identifies sentences containing several independently reviewable claims and recommends separating them so each sentence carries one readily assessable main claim.

relations.reason: The two memories jointly state a reference-only writing tendency and its likely interpretation by readers.
relations.summary: The reference identifies passive phrasing of unsettled commitments as a tendency that can conceal ownership and appear uncertain, evasive, or reluctant.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful reference-only rule about consistent authorial identity, not merely general responsibility attribution.
relations.summary: The reference requires one first-person pronoun for a stable authorial role, changing between “I” and “we” only when the responsible party changes.

relations.reason: These memories split one compared-only operational-feasibility claim into the tracing requirement and the resource dimensions reviewers examine.
relations.summary: The compared frame requires tracing the resources behind prototype features and field procedures because reviewers assess feasibility through required personnel, equipment, and time.

relations.reason: These memories form one compared-only claim linking documentation of external dependencies to readiness assessment and operational variability.
relations.summary: The compared frame requires visible partner commitments, confirmation status, and external field dependencies because schedules and assigned personnel can change beyond researcher control.

reports.both: Both require claims to reflect verification status and responsibility to be attributed explicitly for controlled commitments and deployment work.
reports.compared_only: The compared frame covers feasibility through resource tracing and makes changing partner, personnel, service, and schedule dependencies visible.
reports.reference_only: The reference addresses concise sentence structure, avoiding em dashes, passive commitment language, and inconsistent first-person pronouns.
